newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges Iraq to go the extra mile.
newsitem.headline: France urges Iraq to go the extra mile.

text.p: France urged Iraq on Tuesday to make an extra effort to comply with U.N. Security Council resolutions arising from the Gulf War so that an international economic embargo in force since 1990 could be lifted.

After talks with visiting Iraqi Vice-Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette urged Baghdad to satisfy U.N. inspectors on the removal of its weapons of mass destruction, and make progress on the issue of Kuwaiti and Saudi citizens missing since the 1991 Gulf War.

"I told Mr Tareq Aziz that only Iraq's full cooperation with the U.N. Special Commission and with the International Atomic Energy Authority will make it possible to shed light on the last remaining questions," the French minister said.

"It is clear that an announcement by the Special Commission of positive conclusions concerning Iraq's obligations in the area of weapons of mass destruction is the prior condition for lifting the oil embargo," he said.

De Charette expressed satisfaction that Baghdad had heeded a French appeal during Aziz's last visit to Paris in December 1995 to accept a U.N. resolution allowing it to export limited quantities of oil in exchange for food and medicines for its suffering civilian population.
"In terms of the method, that is a strong encouragement for those such as myself who believe that a determined application of the Security Council resolutions is the right way," he said.
Aziz said he had listened attentively to de Charette and only a small part of the resolutions remained to be implemented.

He said it was important that the application of the resolutions, passed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, should be "fair, balanced and legalistic", and not slanted to meet the desire of "certain countries" -- a clear reference to the United States and Britain.

While France favours bringing Iraq back into the international community as soon as possible, Washington and London appear reluctant to accept any major easing of the embargo as long as President Saddam Hussein remains in power.
The Iraqi minister praised France for its understanding position, illustrated last month when Paris pulled out of joint air patrols with its Gulf War allies over Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.
But de Charette appeared to be determined not to allow Aziz to drive a wedge between France and the Western allies by underlining the need for strict application of the Security Council resolutions.
A French official said Baghdad had "got the message" after Aziz's previous visit to Paris and the French hoped it would "get the message" again this time.
He said there was very little discussion at the meeting of prospects for Franco-Iraqi cooperation after the lifting of the embargo, since this was premature.

French oil companies, which are participating in oil sales under the oil-for-food resolution, have negotiated long-term agreements to help modernise Iraq's petroleum industry once the sanctions are lifted.

Aziz, who met Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Monday, is due to visit Belgium and Spain after meeting French parliament leaders on Wednesday and addressing a leading foreign policy think-tank on Thursday.
France was Iraq's main Western arms supplier before the Gulf War. Baghdad owes Paris more than $5 billion and the French are keen to restore economic ties once the embargo ends.
